entry.summary: Short answer: For a US/EU property-management SaaS, keep signed documents private, send browsers short-lived presigned URLs, and store each deletion deadline in the application database; choose the storage boundary by how much native access control you need, not by upload convenience alone. The boundary is simple: the application authorizes a tenant and issues a narrow transfer grant, the browser moves bytes, and storage holds those bytes until a separate deletion worker acts. This keeps document traffic away from the app server without turning possession of a permanent URL into authorization. It also gives the retention deadline an owner. entry.title: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) for Developers: did:web, did:key and Resolution in Practice
entry.summary: A decentralized identifier (DID) is a URI of the form did:<method>:<method-specific-id> that resolves to a DID document: a JSON object listing public keys and the ways each key may be used. Whoever holds the matching private key can prove they control the DID, with no central identity provider issuing or approving the identifier. That is the whole idea. Everything else (wallets, verifiable credentials, OpenID4VC) is built on top of "resolve an identifier to keys, then verify a signature". This guide skips the blockchain narrative and works through the two methods you will actually meet first, did:key and did:web, with code you can run. entry.title: Is This "15-Second" Hit the Road Dude Clip Actually 15.000 Seconds? Container vs Stream Duration vs Frame Count
entry.summary: The FAQ is blunt: every clip is 15 seconds, vertical 9:16, at 480p or 720p, with sound. That is the product. It is not a length slider, and this is not a note about why the studio ships one length. It is a question about the file you are holding after an edit: do three common clocks — container duration, stream duration, and frame-count divided by fps — actually agree on 15.000 seconds? They often don't. One missing frame at 30 fps is 1/30 s, or 0.033333 s. An edit list can make the container longer than the video stream. A 30000/1001 "30 fps" file can be a clean 15.015 s of picture with 15.000 s of audio. I measured all of that on synthetic 9:16 clips built with ffmpeg 7.1.5. No paid customer renders are used. entry.summary: TL;DR: make the server the authority for lobby presence, give each room a short lease and monotonically increasing epoch, and choose the next host from a deterministic snapshot after a player disconnect. entry.title: How to save and restore browser sessions in Edge or Firefox — the manual ways first
entry.summary: I lose browser sessions the same way everyone does: a restart, a crash, or one careless click on "close all tabs", and the research trail is gone. Before I built anything, I wanted to know what the browsers already do for free — because if the built-in way is good enough, there is nothing to build. Here are the manual ways, tested on current Edge and Firefox. No extension needed. Both browsers have a one-toggle setting for this. Edge: Settings → On startup → "Open tabs from the previous session". Firefox: Settings → General → Startup → "Open previous windows and tabs". This is the cheapest insurance there is. entry.title: "Duplicate URLs: Why One Page Gets Many Addresses"
entry.summary: A page does not have one address. It has as many addresses as clients can construct that resolve to it, and each of those is a separate key in every cache, log, analytics report and access rule that has ever seen it. Most of the confusion people blame on "caching" or "duplicate content" starts here. The specification is precise about which differences matter and which are cosmetic. Practice is less tidy, because servers, proxies and clients each normalise at different points — or not at all. Trailing slash. example.com/about and example.com/about/ are different URLs as far as any cache or log is concerned.
